attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. He quotes Knoop as support, but the replication claim is in his own words.

semantics.note: Faithful. In context, this is about the released o3, as of April 2025.

contract.note: Reading 'readily replicate' as practical reproduction with the released o3 is the ordinary reading the context supports. It does not stretch the claim to fabrication.

evidence.note: ARC Prize report, Apr 22, 2025, inside the window: o3-medium scored 53% on the semi-private v1 set; o3-high returned only 37 of 100 tasks and was judged unscoreable. It also says the production o3 differs from the preview.

reviews.rationale: The independent evaluator could not get a reliable result near 75% from released o3: medium scored 53% and high mostly timed out. That meets the support condition. Marcus's 56% figure is off, but it is not part of this proposition. The report's statement that the December preview was valid does not undercut a claim limited to practical replication.

attribution.note: Marcus summarising his own earlier critique, in his own words.

semantics.note: Faithful. Leaving out 'and more' is harmless.

contract.note: Requiring material methodological defects and distorting omissions is an ordinary reading. Marcus did not say which defects or graphs he meant, so interpretation drives the result.

evidence.note: ARC Prize, Dec 20, 2024: the tested o3 was trained on ARC public training data, and no untrained model was compared. A limitation, but it does not by itself show a design defect.
Competing MIT result (61.9%) predates the demo, but on the public validation set, not the semi-private set. It does not show that a particular graph misled.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no slides or transcript, so the graphs and their stated scope cannot be checked. The missing untrained-model comparison is a limitation, not an established design flaw. Competing work existed but used a different split. The evidence does not settle either half of the claim.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description of recent findings.

contract.note: Plain reading (low full-proof scores across frontier models tested soon after release) is fair and ordinary.

evidence.note: Expert-graded preprint, Apr 9, 2025, before the post: of eight frontier models, all but Gemini scored under 5%, and Gemini averaged 24.4%. Initial tests ran within hours of release.
MAA notice: the 2025 USAMO took place March 19–20, which confirms the problems were fresh. The date alone does not prove no developer had advance access.

reviews.rationale: Expert grading of contemporary frontier models on the newly released 2025 USAMO found very low proof scores. The best model, Gemini, averaged only 24.4%, and the authors themselves describe it as struggling. Testing happened right after the contest, consistent with limited chance to prepare. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. The nearby funding remark is hedged ('if I recall') but is a separate claim.

semantics.note: Faithful, and it adds the FrontierMath context. It claims undisclosed access, not training on answers.

contract.note: Reading nondisclosure as nondisclosure at the time of the announcement is ordinary. The contract names Epoch's public account as an acceptable source.

evidence.note: Epoch statement, Jan 2025, from the counterparty and against its own interest. OpenAI owned the problems and had access to problems and solutions apart from a holdout set. Others needed OpenAI's permission to see them. The data-access arrangement was not clarified at the o3 announcement.

reviews.rationale: Epoch is a party to the agreement, and its account is the source the contract names. It confirms OpenAI had preferential access to problems and solutions that competitors could not get, and that the access arrangement was not disclosed when o3 was announced. Caveat: the livestream transcript was not checked, so this rests on Epoch's admission rather than an independent record. Nothing in the packet contradicts it.
